previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: The patient, a male with a history of alcoholic cirrhosis, hepatitis C, esophageal varices, and chronic alcohol use, was admitted for worsening abdominal pain and reported bright red blood per rectum and in emesis. He had stable vital signs and no active bleeding during the hospitalization. Laboratory results showed anemia with hemoglobin dropping to 8.3 g/dL, elevated INR of 1.5, and mild renal impairment likely due to dehydration. A CT scan revealed an enlarged, fatty liver and non-obstructing renal calculi but no acute abdominal process. The patient was offered endoscopy and medication reconciliation but left against medical advice before procedures or discharge planning could be completed. He acknowledged the risks, including potential fatal hemorrhage, and declined prescriptions despite being advised to follow up within two days.
problems: Esophageal varices without mention of bleeding
Unspecified viral hepatitis C without hepatic coma
Cirrhosis of liver without mention of alcohol
Personal history of noncompliance with medical treatment, presenting hazards to health

Discharge Instructions:
Mr. ___,

It was a pleasure taking care of you during your stay at ___. 
You were admitted for abdominal pain, chest pain, vomiting 
blood, passing blood in your stool, and passing blood in your 
urine. Upper endoscopy showed some gastritis and grade I varices 
that were not bleeding. Colonoscopy showed a few vessel 
malformations that were not bleeding but cauterized by the GI 
team. Hemorrhoids were also seen. Your blood counts remained 
stable throughout admission.

You were also found to have a urinary tract infection and should 
complete a 7 day course of antibiotics. This may be the cause of 
the blood in your urine. If this blood persists after you finish 
your antibiotics, please tell your primary doctor as you may 
require further evaluation.

You were found to have some wheezing on exam and based on your 
history of asthma, were prescribed an albuterol rescue inhaler 
to use if you feel short of breath.

Wishing you well,
Your ___ Medicine Team
